old: they quickly spotted both Kitty and Lydia
new: they quickly spotted, as proof of the coachman's punctuality, both Kitty and Lydia
source: they quickly perceived, in token of the coachman's punctuality, both Kitty and Lydia
reason: The narrator's dry aside (the girls' presence proves the coachman is on time) is dropped entirely.

old: such a plain little freckled thing
new: such a nasty little freckled thing
source: Who _could_ about such a nasty little freckled thing?
reason: "Plain" softens Lydia's insult, yet the next paragraph turns on Elizabeth being shocked by the coarseness of exactly this expression.

old: considered perfectly reasonable!
new: flattered herself was broad-minded!
source: the coarseness of the _sentiment_ was little other than her own breast had formerly harboured and fancied liberal!
reason: "Fancied liberal" means she had congratulated herself on being generous/broad-minded about Wickham's mercenary match; "perfectly reasonable" loses the self-flattery that makes the reproach sting.

old: The comfort of the regiment's approaching departure
new: For her, the comfort of the regiment's approaching departure
source: The comfort to _her_, of the regiment's approaching removal, was indeed beyond expression.
reason: The emphatic "to her" contrasts Elizabeth's relief with her sisters' misery; without it the sentence reads as a general statement.

old: for speaking so harshly about Wickham?
new: for having spoken so warmly in Wickham's favor?
source: But you blame me for having spoken so warmly of Wickham?
reason: "Warmly of" means in his favor (she had championed Wickham against Darcy); "harshly about" reverses the meaning.

old: quite so vain and foolish and absurd
new: quite so weak and vain and absurd
source: that I had not been so very weak, and vain, and nonsensical, as I knew I had!
reason: Elizabeth's self-accusation of weakness is dropped ("foolish and absurd" double up on "nonsensical").

old: isn't rightfully theirs
new: isn't lawfully theirs
source: if they can be easy with an estate that is not lawfully their own
reason: The joke is Mrs. Bennet calling the estate not "lawfully" theirs in the same breath as admitting it is entailed on them by law; "rightfully" blurs the absurdity.

old: as deplorable as such a step would make her look,
new: as detestable as such a step would make her look if it were known,
source: detestable as such a step must make her, were it known, she could not help secretly advising her father
reason: The condition "were it known" (which explains "secretly") is lost, and "detestable" is weakened to "deplorable".

old: harm to us all that must come from Lydia's reckless and imprudent behavior
new: harm to us all that must come from the public notice of Lydia's reckless and imprudent behavior
source: the very great disadvantage to us all, which must arise from the public notice of Lydia's unguarded and imprudent manner
reason: Elizabeth's point is about reputation—the harm comes from Lydia's conduct being publicly noticed; that qualification is dropped.

old: their outrage would have been hard to contain
new: their outrage would have been more than even their combined chatter could express
source: their indignation would hardly have found expression in their united volubility
reason: Austen's joke is that even Lydia and Mrs. Bennet talking together could not have voiced their indignation; "hard to contain" flattens it into a cliché.

old: in the very charm that had first delighted her
new: in the very gentleness that had first delighted her
source: She had even learnt to detect, in the very gentleness which had first delighted her, an affectation
reason: "Gentleness" is the specific quality (echoing Jane's praise of his gentleness in ch. 40) now exposed as affected; "charm" loses it.

old: good terms that she mentioned
new: good terms that, when he asked how she had spent her time at Hunsford, she mentioned
source: that, on his making some inquiry as to the manner in which her time had passed at Hunsford, she mentioned
reason: Wickham's inquiry about Hunsford, which prompts her pointed mention of Fitzwilliam and Darcy, is dropped.

old: and much of it can be traced to his desire
new: and a good deal of his good behavior can be traced to his desire
source: and a good deal is to be imputed to his wish of forwarding the match with Miss de Bourgh
reason: In the candidate "it" now points to "that fear", but Wickham is attributing Darcy's improved conduct (the cautiousness), not his fear, to the de Bourgh match.

old: to seek comfort for his own poor judgment in the pleasures
new: to seek comfort for the disappointment his own poor judgment had brought on in the pleasures
source: to seek comfort for the disappointment which his own imprudence had brought on in any of those pleasures
reason: He seeks comfort for the disappointment, not for his judgment; the compression loses the causal link.

old: blind to the problems in her father's behavior
new: blind to the impropriety of her father's behavior
source: had never been blind to the impropriety of her father's behaviour as a husband
reason: "Impropriety" is a moral and social judgment; "problems" is vaguer and softens Elizabeth's view of her father.

old: Mrs. Gardiner dismissed her excuse.
new: Mrs. Gardiner scolded her for being so silly.
source: Mrs. Gardiner abused her stupidity.
reason: Mrs. Gardiner teasingly calls the objection stupid; "dismissed her excuse" implies she sees through it as an excuse, which the source does not say.

old: In what an unflattering light it might strike so proud a man!
new: In what a disgraceful light it might strike so vain a man!
source: In what a disgraceful light might it not strike so vain a man!
reason: Austen keeps vain and proud distinct (Mary's ch. 5 definition); Elizabeth fears his vanity will read her visit as a pursuit of him. "Unflattering" also softens "disgraceful".

old: they would have been beyond his reach;
new: they would have been out of his sight;
source: they should have been beyond the reach of his discrimination
reason: "Discrimination" means perception/notice: they would have been gone before he could see them. "Beyond his reach" suggests pursuit.

old: the very people whose existence his pride had rejected when he proposed to her
new: the very people his pride had revolted against when he proposed to her
source: some of those very people, against whom his pride had revolted, in his offer to herself
reason: "Whose existence his pride had rejected" is an invented formulation; his pride revolted against the connection with them.

old: but he bore it well,
new: he bore it, however, with fortitude,
source: he sustained it, however, with fortitude
reason: The mock-heroic "with fortitude" (as if meeting a tradesman uncle were an ordeal) is Elizabeth's sly irony; "bore it well" flattens it.

old: we understood you weren't expected in the area at all
new: we understood you weren't expected in the area just yet
source: we understood that you were not immediately expected in the country
reason: "Not immediately expected" becomes "not expected at all", which overstates and contradicts the housekeeper's "tomorrow".

old: had brought him ahead of the rest of his party
new: had brought him a few hours ahead of the rest of his party
source: business with his steward had occasioned his coming forward a few hours before the rest of the party
reason: The "few hours" detail (explaining why he is there a day early) is dropped.

old: were still a good distance behind
new: were an eighth of a mile behind
source: Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner were half a quarter of a mile behind
reason: The specific distance is replaced by a vague phrase; the source's precise, slightly comic measure is dropped.

old: "But he may just be putting on a show of civility," replied her uncle. "Important men often do that.
new: "But perhaps he's a little unpredictable in his civilities," replied her uncle. "Great men often are.
source: "But perhaps he may be a little whimsical in his civilities," replied her uncle. "Your great men often are;
reason: "Whimsical" means changeable, which is why Mr. Gardiner fears being warned off later; "putting on a show" makes him accuse Darcy of insincerity.

old: two or three small incidents before they parted,
new: two or three small incidents occurred before they parted,
source: two or three little circumstances occurred ere they parted
reason: The main verb was dropped, so the sentence is a fragment.

old: free of the arrogance or disdain of his companions
new: free of arrogance or of disdain toward his companions
source: an accent so far removed from _hauteur_ or disdain of his companions
reason: "Disdain of his companions" is Darcy's disdain for the Gardiners; the candidate makes the arrogance belong to the companions.

old: she ventured to say yes for all of them
new: she ventured to accept on her niece's behalf
source: she ventured to engage for her attendance
reason: Mrs. Gardiner commits Elizabeth specifically (whose feelings she could not read), not the party in general.

old: it was now a matter of some importance to Elizabeth to think well of him
new: it was now a matter of some anxiety to them to think well of him
source: Of Mr. Darcy it was now a matter of anxiety to think well
reason: The whole paragraph is the Gardiners' view ("their acquaintance", "They could not be untouched"); the candidate shifts the anxiety to Elizabeth.
